title: AIDA 模型
content: AIDA 模型将广告说服过程划分为吸引注意、激发兴趣、唤起欲望和促成行动四个阶段，常用于分析广告是否具备完整转化链路。 Applicable scenarios: 短视频广告分析; 广告文案评价; 转化路径诊断.
industry_context: 营销理论; 传播模型
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: PAS 痛点解决模型
content: PAS 模型通过指出用户问题、放大问题带来的不便，再提供产品作为解决方案，适合用于高需求导向的广告内容。 Applicable scenarios: 教育广告; 健康管理广告; 工具类产品广告; 生活服务广告.
industry_context: 广告创意; 痛点营销
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: FAB 卖点表达法
content: FAB 方法强调广告应从产品功能出发，解释其相对优势，并最终转化为用户可感知的实际利益。 Applicable scenarios: 产品详情页; 功能型广告; 新品介绍; 技术产品广告.
industry_context: 营销理论; 卖点表达
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 社会认同效应
content: 社会认同效应指消费者会参考他人的选择、评价和使用经验来降低决策不确定性。 Applicable scenarios: 电商广告; 口碑广告; UGC 广告; 达人推荐.
industry_context: 消费者心理; 社会认同
risk_notes: 用户数量等数据应真实可验证
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 稀缺效应
content: 稀缺效应通过强调时间、库存或名额有限来提升用户的紧迫感，从而促进点击或购买行为。 Applicable scenarios: 促销广告; 直播带货; 优惠券领取; 电商大促.
industry_context: 消费者心理; 稀缺效应
risk_notes: 不得虚构库存或活动截止时间
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 场景化广告
content: 场景化广告通过展示产品在具体生活或工作情境中的使用方式，降低用户理解成本并增强代入感。 Applicable scenarios: 家电广告; 食品饮料广告; 本地生活广告; 工具产品广告.
industry_context: 广告创意; 场景化表达
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: UGC 用户证言广告
content: UGC 广告以普通用户的体验、评价或测评作为主要内容，能够提升广告的真实感和可信度。 Applicable scenarios: 美妆广告; 数码测评; 食品试吃; 服务体验.
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 价格锚定
content: 价格锚定通过展示参考价格与当前价格之间的差异，使消费者感知当前报价更具吸引力。 Applicable scenarios: 电商促销; 会员折扣; 课程售卖; 团购广告.
industry_context: 营销理论; 价格策略
risk_notes: 参考价格应具有真实依据
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 绝对化广告表述风险
content: 广告中使用无法证实的绝对化表述可能带来合规风险，例如“全网第一”“唯一有效”“永久解决”等。 Applicable scenarios: 广告文案审核; 生成结果约束; 风险识别.
industry_context: 合规风险; 绝对化用语
source_name: advertising_compliance_common_rule
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 广告营销漏斗
content: 广告营销漏斗将用户从接触广告到最终转化的过程划分为认知、兴趣、考虑、转化和复购等阶段，可用于判断广告内容服务于哪一类投放目标。 Applicable scenarios: 广告目标识别; 素材策略分析; 投放效果解释.
industry_context: 投放目标; 营销漏斗
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 损失规避
content: 损失规避强调人们对损失的敏感度通常高于同等收益，广告可通过“错过成本”强化行动动机。 Applicable scenarios: 限时促销; 会员权益; 课程报名; 新品预约.
industry_context: 消费者心理; 损失规避
risk_notes: 避免恐吓式或过度焦虑式表达
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 权威背书
content: 权威背书通过专家、机构、认证或奖项降低用户的不信任感，提高广告主张的可信度。 Applicable scenarios: 健康广告; 教育广告; 科技产品; 品牌信任建设.
industry_context: 消费者心理; 权威背书
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 情绪共鸣策略
content: 情绪共鸣策略通过亲情、友情、陪伴、梦想或治愈等情绪线索，使受众将产品与情感价值建立联系。 Applicable scenarios: 品牌广告; 节日广告; 公益广告; 高情感商品.
industry_context: 广告创意; 情绪共鸣
risk_notes: 避免与产品功能脱节导致空泛表达
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 视觉隐喻
content: 视觉隐喻通过象征性画面或夸张表达，将抽象卖点转化为可视化形象，例如用闪电表现速度、用盾牌表现安全。 Applicable scenarios: 品牌创意广告; 功能强化广告; 概念产品宣传.
industry_context: 广告创意; 视觉隐喻
risk_notes: 解释隐喻时应回到视频证据
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 前后对比策略
content: 前后对比策略通过展示使用产品前后的状态差异，使产品价值更直观。 Applicable scenarios: 美妆广告; 清洁用品; 健身课程; 工具类产品.
industry_context: 广告创意; 前后对比
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 问题—解决叙事
content: 问题—解决叙事先呈现具体痛点或任务阻碍，再展示产品如何解决问题，适合强调效率、便利或功能价值。 Applicable scenarios: 工具软件; 家居清洁; 生活服务; 办公效率.
industry_context: 广告创意; 问题解决叙事
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 目标受众画像
content: 目标受众画像根据年龄、职业、生活方式、消费需求和使用场景推断广告希望触达的人群。 Applicable scenarios: 受众分析; 投放策略; 素材定向; 内容评估.
industry_context: 受众分析; 人群定位
risk_notes: 受众判断应基于视频中的人物
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 短视频黄金三秒
content: 短视频广告常在开头几秒通过强视觉冲击、问题、悬念或利益点快速吸引注意，以降低划走率。 Applicable scenarios: 信息流广告; 短视频广告; 直播预热视频.
industry_context: 平台内容; 短视频节奏
risk_notes: 钩子应与后续内容一致
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 利益点前置
content: 利益点前置指在广告开头或核心画面中直接呈现用户收益，以提高信息获取效率和转化意愿。 Applicable scenarios: 电商广告; 应用下载广告; 课程广告; 本地生活广告.
industry_context: 广告创意; 利益点前置
risk_notes: 免费等表述需说明条件
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 品牌资产一致性
content: 品牌资产一致性强调在广告中重复使用 Logo、品牌色、口号、包装或吉祥物，帮助受众形成稳定品牌记忆。 Applicable scenarios: 品牌广告; 新品发布; 系列广告; 品牌焕新.
industry_context: 广告创意; 品牌记忆
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: CTA 行动召唤
content: CTA 行动召唤通过明确的动词和路径引导用户完成点击、购买、下载、扫码或领取等行为。 Applicable scenarios: 效果广告; 电商促销; 应用下载; 活动报名.
industry_context: 广告创意; 行动召唤
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 产品特写强化
content: 产品特写通过近距离展示包装、材质、使用细节或效果，强化产品识别和品质感。 Applicable scenarios: 食品饮料; 美妆护肤; 数码产品; 家居用品.
industry_context: 商品表达; 产品特写
risk_notes: 视觉效果不应明显误导实际产品状态
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 旁白卖点强化
content: 旁白或口播常用于补充画面难以直接表达的功能、价格、场景或品牌主张，是广告视频问答中的关键音频证据。 Applicable scenarios: 口播广告; 信息流广告; 产品讲解; 直播切片.
industry_context: 音频表达; 旁白卖点
risk_notes: ASR 噪声会影响证据提取
应结合视觉和 OCR 校验
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 字幕承诺与屏幕文字
content: 广告中的屏幕文字常直接承载价格、优惠、功能承诺和限制条件，回答细节问题时应优先核查 OCR 证据。 Applicable scenarios: 促销广告; 字幕密集广告; 详情讲解; 优惠说明.
industry_context: 文字表达; 字幕承诺
risk_notes: OCR 错误可能导致价格或数字误读
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 功效宣称风险
content: 涉及健康、美妆、教育等领域的功效宣称应基于可验证证据，生成答案时不能将普通宣传语扩展为确定性效果。 Applicable scenarios: 健康广告; 美妆广告; 教育培训; 保健品.
industry_context: 合规风险; 功效宣称
risk_notes: 医疗化或无依据功效表达
source_name: advertising_compliance_common_rule
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 故事化广告叙事
content: 故事化广告通过人物、冲突、转折和结局组织信息，使产品或品牌价值嵌入情节之中。 Applicable scenarios: 品牌广告; 公益广告; 高情感商品; 长视频广告.
industry_context: 内容结构; 故事化叙事
risk_notes: 需区分情节事实与广告寓意
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 反差冲突策略
content: 反差冲突策略通过制造预期与结果之间的差异，引发注意和记忆点，并进一步引出产品价值。 Applicable scenarios: 短视频广告; 喜剧广告; 情节广告; 新品认知.
industry_context: 广告创意; 反差冲突
risk_notes: 反差解释需与视频画面或旁白证据对应
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 用户使用动机
content: 用户使用动机指用户选择产品或服务背后的核心需求，如省时、省钱、提升形象、健康、安全或效率。 Applicable scenarios: 受众需求分析; 卖点归因; 产品定位; 文案评估.
industry_context: 受众分析; 使用动机
risk_notes: 动机推断应结合广告问题
source_name: marketing_common_knowledge
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 证据一致性
content: 证据一致性衡量模型答案中的核心断言是否可由视频帧、ASR、OCR 或检索知识直接支撑。 Applicable scenarios: 链式校验; 人工评分; 幻觉检测; 实验指标.
industry_context: 评价指标; 可解释性
source_name: thesis_evaluation_design
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: 知识一致性
content: 知识一致性衡量模型是否正确使用营销概念，避免将普通促销误判为复杂策略或引入与视频无关的外部知识。 Applicable scenarios: RAG 消融; 人工评分; 营销策略问答; 错误分析.
industry_context: 评价指标; 知识一致性
source_name: thesis_evaluation_design
source_notes: Legacy curated MVP knowledge entry (version=1.1).

title: Close-up Product Priority
content: When an ad repeatedly uses close-ups of a product or a decisive feature, it usually signals that the object itself is the main recall anchor. In video QA, close framing often marks what the advertiser most wants the viewer to notice. QA use: Useful for questions about which visual element is central or most emphasized in the ad.
keywords: brand name spoken during product shot
trigger_features: brand name spoken during product shot
risk_notes: Close-ups can also be stylistic filler if the product is never identified.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Repeated Brand Asset Recall
content: If the logo, pack shape, mascot, or branded color appears early and again later, the ad is probably trying to strengthen brand memory rather than hide the brand until the end. Repetition of brand assets is a strong clue that recall matters. QA use: Useful for questions about brand exposure, brand prominence, or whether the ad is brand-building.
risk_notes: A final end card alone is weaker evidence than repeated in-story branding.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Faces Guide Attention
content: Human faces and gaze direction often act as visual pointers in video ads. When people look at a product, screen text, or another character, the ad is usually guiding viewers toward that same point of attention. QA use: Useful for questions asking what viewers are being guided to notice or how attention is directed visually.
risk_notes: Faces can carry emotion without indicating the most important product cue.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Readable Mobile Visual Pairing
content: On mobile-oriented video, simple visuals paired with short readable text usually indicate a message designed for quick comprehension. Large text plus one dominant visual idea is often more deliberate than crowded multi-claim layouts. QA use: Useful for questions about why the ad looks visually simple or what design choice helps comprehension.
risk_notes: Minimal design can also reflect premium style rather than mobile optimization alone.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Vertical Mobile Framing Signal
content: When framing is clearly vertical, with subjects stacked for phone viewing, the ad is likely designed for mobile-first consumption. This usually means the visual story is being optimized for scrolling environments rather than widescreen immersion. QA use: Useful for questions about format choice, likely platform context, or why the composition feels phone-native.
risk_notes: A vertical crop reused from horizontal video may not reflect an intentional mobile-first design.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Use square and vertical video to engage mobile customers
source_notes: Google recommends square and vertical video plus mobile-friendly framing when advertisers want stronger phone-screen engagement.

title: Square Safe-Zone Composition
content: Square video often keeps the main subject near the center so that important content remains legible across feeds and devices. Centralized composition is therefore a clue that the ad is optimizing portability across placements. QA use: Useful for questions about composition choices and cross-platform video formatting.
risk_notes: Centered layout can also come from generic studio shooting
source_name: Google Ads Help — Use square and vertical video to engage mobile customers
source_notes: Google recommends square and vertical video plus mobile-friendly framing when advertisers want stronger phone-screen engagement.

title: Demonstration Equals Visual Proof
content: A sequence that shows the product being used step by step usually functions as visual proof, not just decoration. Demonstration shots often signal that the advertiser wants the viewer to infer usability or effectiveness from what is shown. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad is demonstrating a feature or merely displaying the product.
risk_notes: A demo montage without clear outcome may show variety rather than proof.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Pack Shot Memory Anchor
content: Repeated pack shots help anchor category memory by tying abstract scenes back to a concrete purchase object. When the product package keeps returning, the advertiser is usually trying to make the brand easy to recognize at shelf or in-app selection. QA use: Useful for questions about why the package is shown multiple times or what object serves as the memory anchor.
keywords: brand name said over pack shot
trigger_features: brand name said over pack shot
risk_notes: A single end-card pack shot is weaker than multiple in-story reappearances.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Split-Screen Comparison Cue
content: Split-screen layouts often cue comparison by reducing the effort needed to judge two states side by side. In ad video reasoning, that format usually implies the viewer is being invited to contrast options, outcomes, or conditions. QA use: Useful for questions about comparison visuals, contrasted scenarios, or what two halves of the screen are meant to communicate.
keywords: contrastive words like before or after
trigger_features: contrastive words like before or after
risk_notes: A split screen can also show simultaneity rather than superiority if no evaluative cue appears.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Tips for optimizing your Video campaign
source_notes: Google connects creative choices, targeting, testing, and calls to action with stronger video-campaign performance.

title: Before-After Transformation Metaphor
content: When the ad moves from a messy, dull, or difficult state to a clean, bright, or easy state, the visual change often works as a metaphor for benefit delivery. Transformation is a common shorthand for improvement. QA use: Useful for questions about symbolic meaning in before-and-after sequences.
risk_notes: The change may represent time passing rather than product effect if no product link is shown.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Light Reveal Means Discovery
content: Reveal shots using beams of light, curtains opening, or hidden objects becoming visible often signal discovery, clarity, or a breakthrough. Such imagery usually points to a meaning beyond literal illumination. QA use: Useful for questions about symbolic visuals or what a reveal sequence implies conceptually.
risk_notes: Light can be purely aesthetic if it is not attached to any claim or change in understanding.
source_name: WARC — The power of storytelling in building brand value
source_notes: WARC highlights how stories, symbols, and meaning-laden narratives can build brand value beyond literal product claims.

title: Shield Imagery Implies Protection
content: Visuals such as shields, locks, barriers, or protective bubbles often stand for safety, reliability, or defense from harm. In ad QA, these symbols usually indicate the promised role of the product rather than literal equipment. QA use: Useful for questions about symbolic objects and what abstract benefit they represent.
risk_notes: Some categories literally sell security products
so the symbol may be functional rather than metaphorical.
source_name: McGraw Hill — Advertising and Promotion (Belch) public textbook page
source_notes: The public textbook summary points to standard integrated marketing communication principles for branding, persuasion, targeting, and response.

title: Journey Visual Means Progress
content: Roads, paths, stairways, and forward motion often symbolize progress, advancement, or a life transition. When these visuals frame the product story, the ad is often attaching the brand to personal growth or momentum. QA use: Useful for questions about recurring travel imagery or what movement signifies beyond travel itself.
risk_notes: Travel categories may use roads literally
source_name: WARC — The power of storytelling in building brand value
source_notes: WARC highlights how stories, symbols, and meaning-laden narratives can build brand value beyond literal product claims.

title: Color Palette Sets Mood Fast
content: Color often establishes mood before the message is fully understood. Warm palettes can feel intimate or energetic, while cool palettes can feel calm, clean, or technical depending on the surrounding cues. QA use: Useful for questions about atmosphere, mood, or why the ad feels warm, calm, premium, or clinical.
keywords: voice tone aligns with color mood
trigger_features: voice tone aligns with color mood
risk_notes: Color meaning changes by category and culture
so palette alone should not decide the full message.
source_name: Nielsen — Advertising emotions increase sales
source_notes: Nielsen argues that ad-evoked emotion is an important driver of connection and sales response, especially in cluttered media environments.

title: Fast-Cut Montage Means Energy
content: Rapid cuts across multiple scenes often suggest pace, variety, and high energy rather than detailed explanation. In video QA, a fast montage usually means the ad wants the viewer to feel momentum more than inspect a single feature deeply. QA use: Useful for questions about editing pace, energetic atmosphere, or why many scenes appear quickly.
risk_notes: Fast edits can also be used to compress information in tutorials
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Safe-Area Legibility Matters
content: If text, logos, and buttons stay large and central with clear margins, the creative is probably respecting format constraints and safe areas. This is a cue that the ad is designed to remain legible across placements, crops, and device interfaces. QA use: Useful for questions about layout discipline, mobile legibility, or why elements avoid the edges of frame.
risk_notes: Minimal layouts can come from brand style
source_name: Google Ads Help — Google Ads specs: ad formats, sizes, and best practices
source_notes: Google’s specs page supports rules about aspect ratio, safe framing, legibility, and asset-format constraints.

title: Warm Social Scenes Cue Belonging
content: Scenes of shared meals, hugs, teamwork, or family routines often aim to evoke belonging and social comfort. In advertising, this emotional route can make the brand feel personally relevant even when product information is light. QA use: Useful for questions about what emotion the ad is trying to evoke and why people are shown together.
keywords: inclusive wording like together or share
trigger_features: inclusive wording like together or share
risk_notes: Group scenes can show usage context without strongly targeting belonging if emotion is muted.
source_name: Nielsen — Advertising emotions increase sales
source_notes: Nielsen argues that ad-evoked emotion is an important driver of connection and sales response, especially in cluttered media environments.

title: Surprise Breaks Through Clutter
content: Unexpected visual twists, abrupt reveals, or unusual scene changes often function to break attention inertia. Surprise is especially useful when the ad must win attention quickly in crowded viewing environments. QA use: Useful for questions about why the ad uses an odd opening, abrupt reveal, or incongruous image.
risk_notes: Shock alone does not prove persuasion if the brand or message never reconnects to the surprise.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Humor Lowers Resistance
content: Humor can make a sales message feel less like a hard push and more like entertainment, which lowers resistance to the ad. The effect is stronger when the joke clearly connects back to the product or brand point. QA use: Useful for questions about whether humor is being used as a persuasion or emotional device.
risk_notes: A funny scene that never links back to the brand may create entertainment without strong selling impact.
source_name: Nielsen — Advertising emotions increase sales
source_notes: Nielsen argues that ad-evoked emotion is an important driver of connection and sales response, especially in cluttered media environments.

title: Relief Marks Solution Arrival
content: If the ad first shows frustration, stress, or inconvenience and then shifts to calm or ease, the emotional pivot usually marks the moment when the product is positioned as the solution. Relief is a common signal of problem resolution. QA use: Useful for questions about emotional change over time or what feeling the product is meant to resolve.
risk_notes: Mood improvement may come from scene change alone if the product is not causally linked.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Aspirational Lifestyle Appeal
content: Polished lifestyle scenes often aim to trigger aspiration by showing the viewer who they could be, not just what they could buy. This emotional route attaches the brand to identity and self-image. QA use: Useful for questions about aspirational tone, idealized settings, or lifestyle-based emotional appeal.
risk_notes: Premium visuals can also reflect category norms rather than a strong aspirational strategy.
source_name: Kantar — Creative consumer connections: how to reach your consumers
source_notes: Kantar emphasizes consumer resonance, context, and relevance when matching creative to audience motivations and situations.

title: Calm Tone Builds Trust
content: Slow pacing, stable shots, and calm music often support feelings of trust, reassurance, and care. This is especially common in categories where the advertiser wants to reduce anxiety or signal reliability. QA use: Useful for questions about why an ad feels reassuring, trustworthy, or emotionally gentle.
risk_notes: Calm execution can also signal premium luxury rather than trust alone.
source_name: Nielsen — Advertising emotions increase sales
source_notes: Nielsen argues that ad-evoked emotion is an important driver of connection and sales response, especially in cluttered media environments.

title: Upbeat Tempo Signals Excitement
content: Fast music, quick rhythmic edits, and bright movement often prime excitement before the viewer processes all the copy. Sensory energy can therefore be a deliberate emotional mechanism rather than mere style. QA use: Useful for questions about energetic mood, excitement, or why the ad feels lively and youthful.
risk_notes: A high-tempo soundtrack can clash with a serious message
source_name: Nielsen — Advertising emotions increase sales
source_notes: Nielsen argues that ad-evoked emotion is an important driver of connection and sales response, especially in cluttered media environments.

title: Sensory Closeups Increase Vividness
content: Close shots of texture, steam, sparkle, or physical interaction can make the experience feel more vivid, almost like a simulated trial. This often strengthens emotional immediacy even when the viewer cannot actually touch or taste the product. QA use: Useful for questions about why texture, sound, or tactile detail is emphasized.
risk_notes: Sensory detail can also be decorative if it never connects to a clear benefit.
source_name: Kantar — The art of proof: how creative quality drives profit
source_notes: Kantar links creative quality and clarity of proof to stronger business results, supporting rules about concrete evidence and branded creativity.

title: Voice Tone Changes Meaning
content: The same visual sequence can feel playful, urgent, or sincere depending on the voiceover tone. In ad-video reasoning, vocal delivery is often a key clue for emotional framing when visuals are ambiguous. QA use: Useful for questions about how audio changes the interpretation of the same imagery.
risk_notes: Music and on-screen text can override voice tone if they strongly conflict.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Celebration Signals Shared Joy
content: Crowd applause, cheering, and group celebration often cue shared joy and social validation. This emotional device suggests that the product or brand belongs in moments of public success or communal happiness. QA use: Useful for questions about celebratory emotion or why groups are shown reacting together.
risk_notes: Crowds can also indicate popularity rather than pure joy if proof claims are foregrounded.
source_name: Nielsen — Advertising emotions increase sales
source_notes: Nielsen argues that ad-evoked emotion is an important driver of connection and sales response, especially in cluttered media environments.

title: Quiet Soundscape Cues Sincerity
content: When music drops back and room tone or small sounds become noticeable, the ad often signals sincerity, honesty, or emotional intimacy. A quieter soundscape can make the moment feel more personal and less performative. QA use: Useful for questions about intimate emotional tone or why the ad suddenly becomes quieter.
risk_notes: Silence can also build suspense rather than sincerity if the scene is tense.
source_name: IPA EffWorks — The Power of Emotion
source_notes: IPA/EffWorks summarizes evidence that emotion is a major mechanism behind campaign effectiveness and long-term impact.

title: Nostalgia Evokes Comfort
content: Retro props, childhood settings, or familiar rituals often trigger nostalgia, which can create comfort and affection toward the brand. Nostalgia works by linking the ad to a remembered emotional world rather than a purely rational claim. QA use: Useful for questions about retro styling, memory-based emotion, or why the ad uses old-fashioned cues.
risk_notes: Vintage styling may sometimes be used only as fashion rather than true nostalgia.
source_name: WARC — The power of storytelling in building brand value
source_notes: WARC highlights how stories, symbols, and meaning-laden narratives can build brand value beyond literal product claims.

title: Tension Then Release Intensifies Payoff
content: Ads often amplify feeling by first creating tension and then resolving it. The emotional payoff usually feels stronger because the viewer has been led through a mini-arc rather than shown a flat positive scene throughout. QA use: Useful for questions about emotional progression or why the ad begins with friction before a positive ending.
keywords: voiceover changes from tense to calm
trigger_features: voiceover changes from tense to calm
risk_notes: The release may come from narrative coincidence rather than the product if the link is weak.
source_name: IPA EffWorks — The Power of Emotion
source_notes: IPA/EffWorks summarizes evidence that emotion is a major mechanism behind campaign effectiveness and long-term impact.

title: Reaction Shots Create Empathy
content: Close reaction shots of people noticing, tasting, or benefiting from something help viewers simulate that feeling themselves. Empathy is often built through visible human response rather than verbal explanation. QA use: Useful for questions about why reactions are emphasized or how the ad tries to make viewers feel alongside characters.
risk_notes: Reaction shots without cause can feel generic and less persuasive.
source_name: Kantar — Creative consumer connections: how to reach your consumers
source_notes: Kantar emphasizes consumer resonance, context, and relevance when matching creative to audience motivations and situations.

title: Expert Presence Reduces Perceived Risk
content: When an ad shows a relevant expert, professional environment, or institutional cue, it borrows credibility to make the claim feel safer to accept. In higher-stakes categories, this authority effect works as a form of credibility transfer. QA use: Useful for questions about expert endorsement, why a professional appears on screen, or how the ad tries to make a serious claim feel safer to trust.
risk_notes: If the authority figure seems irrelevant to the claim
the cue is weaker and can feel staged.
source_name: McGraw Hill — Advertising and Promotion (Belch) public textbook page
source_notes: The public textbook summary points to standard integrated marketing communication principles for branding, persuasion, targeting, and response.

title: Humor Must Link Back to Brand
content: Humor helps most when the joke naturally reinforces the product idea or brand role. If the laugh is memorable but the brand point is not, the ad risks entertainment without durable persuasion. QA use: Useful for questions about whether humor supports or distracts from the ad’s commercial message.
keywords: funny situation tied to product use
trigger_features: funny situation tied to product use
risk_notes: A very funny cold open may overshadow the brand if branding arrives too late.
source_name: Kantar — The art of proof: how creative quality drives profit
source_notes: Kantar links creative quality and clarity of proof to stronger business results, supporting rules about concrete evidence and branded creativity.

title: Single Message Discipline
content: If one phrase, image cluster, or benefit keeps recurring while competing claims are absent, the ad is probably organized around one main takeaway. Repetition is a practical clue for extracting the core message. QA use: Useful for questions asking for the ad’s main message or central takeaway.
keywords: same words in VO and text
trigger_features: same words in VO and text
risk_notes: Some minimal ads are ambiguous on purpose
so repetition matters more than simplicity alone.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Benefit-Led Headline Reveals Message
content: When the first major text line states a result or user benefit, that headline usually reveals the intended message more directly than surrounding scene details. Benefit-led copy is a strong summary cue. QA use: Useful for questions about headline meaning, key promise, or the ad’s intended takeaway.
risk_notes: A flashy line may be only a hook if later scenes clearly replace it with another claim.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Tagline Signals Positioning
content: A memorable tagline often compresses the brand’s desired position into a short verbal cue. When it is repeated or given special emphasis, it can be treated as a direct hint to the intended brand meaning. QA use: Useful for questions about slogans, brand claims, or what the advertiser wants the brand to stand for.
risk_notes: Some slogans are generic and need visual context before they can be interpreted reliably.
source_name: McGraw Hill — Advertising and Promotion (Belch) public textbook page
source_notes: The public textbook summary points to standard integrated marketing communication principles for branding, persuasion, targeting, and response.

title: Early Brand Plus Benefit Signals Awareness Goal
content: If the ad introduces the brand quickly and ties it to one easy-to-grasp benefit, the likely aim is broad awareness rather than deep explanation. Early brand-plus-benefit pairing is often optimized for memory under short viewing time. QA use: Useful for questions about likely objective, especially when the ad feels broad and easy to remember.
risk_notes: A direct-response ad can also brand early
so urgency and offer cues must be checked separately.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Problem-to-Solution Story Reveals Message
content: A mini-story that begins with a recognizable problem and ends in a better state usually implies that the product’s core message is problem resolution. The solved state often tells you what the advertiser thinks matters most. QA use: Useful for questions about narrative meaning, solution message, or story-based theme extraction.
risk_notes: Some stories are image-building and use problems only loosely
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Repeated Use-Case Cues Show Core Purpose
content: When the same use case appears across multiple scenes, the advertiser is often trying to make one practical purpose unmistakable. Repetition of context is therefore a clue to the product’s core job-to-be-done. QA use: Useful for questions about intended use case, practical function, or product purpose.
keywords: feature callouts tied to one task
trigger_features: feature callouts tied to one task
risk_notes: Multiple scenarios can instead indicate broad versatility if the benefit is abstract.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Tips for optimizing your Video campaign
source_notes: Google connects creative choices, targeting, testing, and calls to action with stronger video-campaign performance.

title: Distinctive Brand Codes Build Memory
content: Consistent use of brand colors, shapes, mascots, or sonic signatures suggests the ad is investing in distinctive memory structures, not just short-term information transfer. These codes often signal long-term brand building. QA use: Useful for questions about why certain branded colors or symbols keep appearing and what strategic role they play.
risk_notes: Some category conventions resemble brand codes
source_name: Kantar — The art of proof: how creative quality drives profit
source_notes: Kantar links creative quality and clarity of proof to stronger business results, supporting rules about concrete evidence and branded creativity.

title: Atmosphere-Heavy Ads Sell Meaning
content: If the ad spends more time creating mood, identity, or symbolic atmosphere than listing features, the central message is often about brand meaning rather than product detail. This is common when the brand wants to stand for a feeling or worldview. QA use: Useful for questions about image-building themes or why the ad feels more atmospheric than informational.
risk_notes: Luxury and fashion categories often use atmosphere by default
source_name: WARC — The power of storytelling in building brand value
source_notes: WARC highlights how stories, symbols, and meaning-laden narratives can build brand value beyond literal product claims.

title: Feature Labels Point to Practical Message
content: On-screen labels, callouts, and explicit feature naming usually indicate a practical explanatory message rather than pure image-building. Clear labeling is often a sign the advertiser expects viewers to compare or evaluate. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad is educational, feature-focused, or meant to help product evaluation.
risk_notes: Labels can also be decorative in tech categories if no benefit is attached.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Tips for optimizing your Video campaign
source_notes: Google connects creative choices, targeting, testing, and calls to action with stronger video-campaign performance.

title: Offer Cluster Signals Transactional Message
content: When price, promotion, limited-time language, and a direct action prompt appear together, the ad’s main message is usually transactional rather than purely expressive. The ad is trying to move the viewer toward action now. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad is sales-driven or conversion-focused.
risk_notes: Some awareness ads mention price lightly
but dense offer clustering is stronger evidence of conversion focus.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Tips for optimizing your Video campaign
source_notes: Google connects creative choices, targeting, testing, and calls to action with stronger video-campaign performance.

title: Repeated Promise Defines Takeaway
content: If both the narration and the text keep reinforcing the same promise, that promise is probably the intended takeaway even if the visual story varies. Cross-channel repetition is a strong message extraction cue. QA use: Useful for questions about the core promise when visuals show several different situations.
keywords: different scenes but same promise text
trigger_features: different scenes but same promise text
risk_notes: the ad may be intentionally ambiguous or poorly aligned.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Brand as Life Enabler
content: When the product appears inside a broader life moment instead of dominating the frame alone, the brand is often being positioned as an enabler of a desired lifestyle or emotion. The message is about what the brand helps make possible. QA use: Useful for questions about the brand’s role in the story and what the product symbolizes in context.
risk_notes: Some low-branding ads may simply under-show the product rather than intentionally cast it as an enabler.
source_name: Kantar — Creative consumer connections: how to reach your consumers
source_notes: Kantar emphasizes consumer resonance, context, and relevance when matching creative to audience motivations and situations.

title: Educational Tone Signals Research Stage
content: A teaching or explanatory tone often indicates that the advertiser expects viewers to be gathering information, not just recognizing the brand. Educational framing is therefore a clue to consideration-stage messaging. QA use: Useful for questions about funnel stage, explanatory tone, or why the ad includes guidance and detail.
keywords: phrases like learn how or here is how
trigger_features: phrases like learn how or here is how
risk_notes: Educational tone can also support onboarding for existing users
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Community Language Signals Loyalty
content: Words like join, subscribe, member, or stay with us often suggest the advertiser is building an ongoing relationship rather than pushing a one-time purchase alone. This language is a clue that loyalty or community is part of the message. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad seeks recurring engagement, membership, or long-term brand relationship.
risk_notes: Some acquisition ads borrow community language without meaning true loyalty-building.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: One Promise Across Many Scenes
content: If many different scenes all resolve into the same promised benefit, the ad is often trying to show that one value proposition travels across contexts. Breadth of scenario can therefore reinforce, not dilute, a single theme. QA use: Useful for questions about why diverse scenes still point to one main idea.
keywords: same benefit phrase in each scene
trigger_features: same benefit phrase in each scene
risk_notes: Multiple scenes can also imply multiple audiences
so the repeated promise must be clear.
source_name: McGraw Hill — Advertising and Promotion (Belch) public textbook page
source_notes: The public textbook summary points to standard integrated marketing communication principles for branding, persuasion, targeting, and response.

title: Symbolic Imagery Often Means Image-Building
content: Abstract symbolic scenes with sparse literal explanation often indicate image-building rather than detailed selling. In such cases, the theme is usually inferred from mood, metaphor, and brand association rather than feature detail. QA use: Useful for questions about abstract ads, symbolic storytelling, or why the message seems indirect.
risk_notes: Some symbolic ads still contain a direct CTA at the end
so the broader structure should be checked.
source_name: WARC — The power of storytelling in building brand value
source_notes: WARC highlights how stories, symbols, and meaning-laden narratives can build brand value beyond literal product claims.

title: Problem-Solution Persuasion Pattern
content: A common persuasion structure is to surface a familiar pain point and then resolve it with the product. This pattern works by making the need salient before presenting the answer. QA use: Useful for questions about persuasion strategy, especially whether the ad uses pain-point framing.
risk_notes: A problem scene can sometimes be comic setup rather than serious persuasion if the solution is vague.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Side-by-Side Contrast Simplifies Choice
content: Persuasion often becomes easier when the ad lets viewers compare two states at the same time. A side-by-side setup lowers mental effort and makes improvement easier to judge quickly. QA use: Useful for questions about comparison strategy, contrast framing, or why simultaneous visuals are used.
keywords: phrases like more than or less than
trigger_features: phrases like more than or less than
risk_notes: Not every two-panel layout implies superiority
some show two use cases instead.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Tips for optimizing your Video campaign
source_notes: Google connects creative choices, targeting, testing, and calls to action with stronger video-campaign performance.

title: Social Proof Reduces Risk
content: Ratings, testimonials, visible crowds, or “people like you” evidence work as social proof because they reduce uncertainty about trying the product. The persuasive logic is borrowed trust from other users. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad uses testimonials, reviews, or popularity as persuasion.
risk_notes: Crowds can also be used for mood or excitement without explicit proof intent.
source_name: McGraw Hill — Advertising and Promotion (Belch) public textbook page
source_notes: The public textbook summary points to standard integrated marketing communication principles for branding, persuasion, targeting, and response.

title: Authority Cue Strengthens Credibility
content: Experts, professionals, or institutional settings can strengthen persuasion by signaling competence and reliability. This is especially useful when the claim is technical, health-related, or otherwise high-stakes. QA use: Useful for questions about expert endorsement, authority-based persuasion, or why uniforms and professional settings appear.
risk_notes: An authority figure who seems irrelevant to the claim can weaken rather than strengthen persuasion.
source_name: McGraw Hill — Advertising and Promotion (Belch) public textbook page
source_notes: The public textbook summary points to standard integrated marketing communication principles for branding, persuasion, targeting, and response.

title: Concrete Proof Beats Vague Superlatives
content: Specific numbers, demonstrations, or concrete evidence usually persuade better than empty superlatives because they give the viewer something more evaluable. Clear proof cues often signal a deliberate rational persuasion route. QA use: Useful for questions about why the ad uses figures, measurements, or concrete comparisons.
risk_notes: Precise-looking numbers can still be weak if the ad gives no source or visual support.
source_name: Kantar — The art of proof: how creative quality drives profit
source_notes: Kantar links creative quality and clarity of proof to stronger business results, supporting rules about concrete evidence and branded creativity.

title: Demo Functions as Proof
content: Showing the product work in context often persuades more effectively than merely saying it works. In ad interpretation, demonstration is a clue that proof-by-performance is part of the strategy. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad persuades through demonstration or through assertion alone.
risk_notes: A fast demo montage can look like lifestyle footage if the result is not clearly visible.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Tips for optimizing your Video campaign
source_notes: Google connects creative choices, targeting, testing, and calls to action with stronger video-campaign performance.

title: Direct CTA Clarifies Next Step
content: A strong ad often tells viewers exactly what to do next instead of leaving the response implicit. Imperative CTA language is therefore a key clue that the persuasion strategy is trying to convert attention into action. QA use: Useful for questions about calls to action, conversion intent, or response-oriented persuasion.
risk_notes: A brand slogan can sound imperative without truly being a CTA if no response path is shown.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Visual Plus Verbal CTA Is Stronger
content: When a CTA is both shown on screen and spoken aloud, the response path becomes harder to miss. Dual-modality direction is often a deliberate strategy in short or distracting viewing contexts. QA use: Useful for questions about how strongly the ad pushes an action or why the CTA is repeated in multiple forms.
keywords: spoken CTA timed to final frame
trigger_features: spoken CTA timed to final frame
risk_notes: Repeated CTA can feel pushy if it arrives before the value proposition is clear.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Soft CTA Fits Mid-Funnel Persuasion
content: Calls such as learn more, watch more, or explore are softer than buy now and usually fit persuasion aimed at continuing interest rather than immediate purchase. The ad is often trying to keep the viewer moving rather than closing the deal instantly. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the CTA suggests consideration rather than direct conversion.
risk_notes: A soft CTA can appear in awareness ads too
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Urgency Pushes Direct Response
content: Limited-time phrases, countdown-like cues, and seasonal offer windows are classic urgency signals. When they cluster around the CTA, the ad is usually trying to compress decision time and increase immediate response. QA use: Useful for questions about urgency, deadline pressure, or why the ad feels sales-activated.
risk_notes: Seasonal timing alone does not always imply urgency unless the action window is emphasized.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Tips for optimizing your Video campaign
source_notes: Google connects creative choices, targeting, testing, and calls to action with stronger video-campaign performance.

title: Repeat the Ask Near the End
content: In short video, repeating the ask close to the end helps capture viewers who stayed long enough to be interested. The repeated final prompt usually indicates that closing clarity matters more than subtlety. QA use: Useful for questions about why the ad repeats its CTA or why the end card resembles the earlier prompt.
keywords: same CTA returns on end card
trigger_features: same CTA returns on end card
risk_notes: If the repeated prompt is only a tagline
it may support memory rather than action.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Use the Old State as a Foil
content: Persuasion often gets stronger when the ad contrasts the product with an older, slower, messier, or more frustrating state. The previous state acts as a foil that makes the benefit feel larger. QA use: Useful for questions about contrast strategy or why the ad spends time on a bad old method.
keywords: phrases like no more or instead of
trigger_features: phrases like no more or instead of
risk_notes: If the old state is exaggerated too heavily
the contrast may be humorous more than literal.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Sensory Detail Can Stand In for Trial
content: Because viewers cannot physically try the product, ads often use texture, sound, and reaction shots as a proxy for trial experience. Sensory proof can therefore function as persuasion, not just decoration. QA use: Useful for questions about why texture, sound, or tactile detail is central to the ad’s selling strategy.
risk_notes: Sensory detail is less persuasive if the category value is mainly abstract or financial.
source_name: Kantar — The art of proof: how creative quality drives profit
source_notes: Kantar links creative quality and clarity of proof to stronger business results, supporting rules about concrete evidence and branded creativity.

title: Urgency Visuals Signal Action Focus
content: Countdown styling, flashing offer cards, checkout-style end cards, and prominent price framing usually mean the ad is optimized for direct response. The creative is signaling that immediate action matters more than long reflection. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the persuasion strategy is conversion-oriented or sales-activated.
risk_notes: An awareness ad can mention a product launch date without truly being direct response.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Tips for optimizing your Video campaign
source_notes: Google connects creative choices, targeting, testing, and calls to action with stronger video-campaign performance.

title: Brand-Linked Surprise Persuades Better Than Random Gimmicks
content: Surprise, humor, or novelty work better when they make the brand idea more memorable instead of floating separately as a gimmick. Persuasion improves when the creative twist naturally resolves into the selling point. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad’s surprise device meaningfully serves persuasion.
risk_notes: Pure spectacle may win attention but fail to support message retention.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About the ABCDs of effective video ads
source_notes: Google’s ABCD framework stresses early attention, visible branding, emotional connection, and clear direction in video advertising.

title: Skippable Formats Need Early Clarity
content: When a format lets viewers skip or move on quickly, the ad usually needs to front-load the hook, brand, or core benefit instead of saving all meaning for the end. Format pressure often shapes persuasion strategy. QA use: Useful for questions about why the ad opens quickly, brands early, or compresses its pitch into the first moments.
risk_notes: Some short ads brand early for recall even when the format is not skippable.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About video ad formats
source_notes: Google’s video format guidance helps map length, placement, skip behavior, and response style to likely creative strategy.

title: Lifestyle Props Reveal Affinity Audience
content: Props, hobbies, and repeated lifestyle markers often suggest an affinity-style audience defined by enduring interests rather than one immediate purchase task. The ad is signaling who naturally identifies with the scene. QA use: Useful for questions about likely target audience or what long-term interests the ad assumes.
risk_notes: Some props are generic scene fillers
so repeated lifestyle patterns are stronger evidence.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About affinity segments
source_notes: Google describes affinity segments as durable interest and lifestyle groupings useful for awareness and consideration.

title: Search-Like Language Suggests In-Market Intent
content: When the copy sounds like a problem someone is actively trying to solve, the ad often targets in-market or high-intent viewers. Task-focused wording is a clue that the audience may already be evaluating options. QA use: Useful for questions about audience readiness or whether the ad targets active shoppers rather than broad awareness.
risk_notes: Some broad campaigns borrow search-like wording to look relevant without strict high intent.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Use the Audience builder when creating a campaign
source_notes: Google explains that audience builder combines demographics, first-party lists, interests, search-term cues, and AI-based signals.

title: Household Routine Implies Family Decision-Maker
content: Ads built around family logistics, home routines, or care responsibilities often imply an audience involved in household decisions. The target is less about age alone and more about role in daily coordination. QA use: Useful for questions about likely household role or family-oriented target audience.
risk_notes: Not every family scene targets parents specifically
some may aim at broad warmth and belonging.
source_name: Kantar — Creative consumer connections: how to reach your consumers
source_notes: Kantar emphasizes consumer resonance, context, and relevance when matching creative to audience motivations and situations.

title: Use-Case Context Reveals Segment
content: Commuting, studying, traveling, gym sessions, and similar contexts often act as audience segmentation cues because they show the moments in which the product matters. Repeated context can therefore identify the intended user group. QA use: Useful for questions about what type of person or daily situation the ad is built around.
risk_notes: A single context shot may be illustrative rather than audience-defining if other cues point elsewhere.
source_name: Kantar — Creative consumer connections: how to reach your consumers
source_notes: Kantar emphasizes consumer resonance, context, and relevance when matching creative to audience motivations and situations.

title: Premium Cues Suggest Status Audience
content: Polished cinematography, scarce clutter, upscale settings, and restrained pricing emphasis often suggest a status- or identity-oriented audience. The ad assumes the viewer cares about symbolic value as well as function. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the target audience is premium, status-seeking, or image-conscious.
risk_notes: Premium aesthetics can appear in mid-market categories as aspiration rather than actual high-end targeting.

source_notes: The public textbook summary points to standard integrated marketing communication principles for branding, persuasion, targeting, and response.

title: Savings Emphasis Suggests Value Audience
content: When an ad foregrounds price cuts, bundles, or money-saving outcomes, it often targets a value-sensitive audience segment. The creative assumes economic utility is central to the viewer’s decision. QA use: Useful for questions about budget-conscious audiences or why the ad highlights savings so aggressively.
risk_notes: Even premium brands may spotlight a sale temporarily
so repeated value cues matter more than a single discount.

title: Tutorial Tone Fits Information-Seeking Viewers
content: If the ad explains usage step by step, it likely assumes the viewer is still learning and comparing options rather than already convinced. Tutorial framing is therefore a strong clue for consideration-stage reasoning. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the creative targets viewers who are still researching, learning the product, or seeking reassurance before acting.
risk_notes: Some onboarding ads are for existing customers
so other audience cues should be checked.

source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Vertical Punchy Creative Fits Scroll Audiences
content: Short, punchy, vertically framed creative is often designed for viewers who encounter the ad while scrolling on phones. The audience assumption is limited attention and a feed-native viewing posture. QA use: Useful for questions about likely platform behavior or why the ad is structured for fast mobile engagement.
risk_notes: Some vertical videos are repurposed from stories or shorts without a strong targeting implication.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Use square and vertical video to engage mobile customers
source_notes: Google recommends square and vertical video plus mobile-friendly framing when advertisers want stronger phone-screen engagement.

title: Broad Storytelling Often Signals Reach Objective
content: When an ad uses broad emotional storytelling and avoids niche technical detail, it often points to a wide-reach awareness objective rather than narrow specialist targeting. The audience is likely larger and more heterogeneous. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad is trying to reach a broad public or a niche expert group.
risk_notes: Some mass-market categories still use technical proof later in the ad
source_name: IPA — The Long and the Short of It
source_notes: IPA distinguishes between short-term sales activation and long-term brand building, useful for inferring likely funnel intent.

title: Broad Benefit Language Supports Adjacent Segments
content: When creative uses one clear benefit that makes sense to several neighboring segments, it can target a core audience without becoming too narrow for adjacent viewers. Broadly legible benefit language is a clue that the advertiser wants scalable relevance. QA use: Useful for questions about why an ad feels broader than a tiny niche audience, even when some audience cues look specific.
keywords: specific audience hints with broad benefit framing
one clear benefit across varied scenes
trigger_features: specific audience hints with broad benefit framing
one clear benefit across varied scenes
risk_notes: Broad language alone does not prove expansion intent if the rest of the creative is highly niche.
source_name: Google Ads Help — Use the Audience builder when creating a campaign
source_notes: Google explains that audience builder combines demographics, first-party lists, interests, search-term cues, and AI-based signals.

title: Affinity Themes Suggest Long-Term Interest
content: If the ad leans heavily on hobbies, passions, and identity-laden themes, it is often speaking to long-term interests rather than immediate purchase urgency. This is a clue toward awareness or early consideration audiences. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the audience is defined by lifestyle identity rather than active buying intent.
risk_notes: Some hobby-themed ads still chase conversion if strong offers are also present.
source_name: Google Ads Help — About affinity segments
source_notes: Google describes affinity segments as durable interest and lifestyle groupings useful for awareness and consideration.

title: Welcome-Back Language Suggests Retention Audience
content: When the ad assumes prior familiarity, using cues like welcome back, upgrade, reorder, or member benefits, it often targets existing customers or lapsed users rather than first-time prospects. The intended audience already knows the brand. QA use: Useful for questions about retention, loyalty, or whether the viewer is presumed to be an existing user.
risk_notes: A generic app reminder can resemble retention messaging without true customer targeting.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Many People, One Promise Means Scalable Relevance
content: If the ad shows different people or settings but keeps returning to one shared benefit, it is often trying to scale reach without changing the core promise. Diversity of context can therefore signal a broad-reach objective rather than message confusion. QA use: Useful for questions about whether the ad is trying to reach a broad audience with one promise instead of speaking only to a narrow niche.
risk_notes: Casting diversity alone is not enough
the same benefit must clearly unite the scenes.

title: Platform-Native CTA Reveals Audience Context
content: Calls such as subscribe, follow, watch next, or learn more often reflect the norms of the platform and the expected audience behavior there. The CTA can therefore reveal the kind of viewing context the advertiser assumes. QA use: Useful for questions about likely platform environment or why the action requested is not immediate purchase.
risk_notes: Some ecommerce brands borrow creator-style language without living mainly in creator ecosystems.
source_name: YouTube Help — Tips for creating effective video ads
source_notes: YouTube guidance highlights storytelling, curiosity-driven hooks, contextual relevance, and platform-appropriate viewer actions.

title: Signal-Based Delivery Requires Broadly Readable Branding
content: When delivery systems may expand beyond the seed audience, broadly readable branding becomes even more important because not every viewer shares the same prior context. Clear brand assets help adjacent audiences understand who is speaking quickly. QA use: Useful for questions about why branding is extra explicit in otherwise broad audience-targeted creative.
risk_notes: Strong branding can also simply reflect category competition

title: Motivation Cues Beat Demographics
content: Audience inference is often stronger from repeated goals, routines, and passions than from visible age or appearance alone. Ads tend to segment around motivations and use contexts, not just demographics. QA use: Useful for questions about inferred audience motivation, likely lifestyle cluster, or why an ad emphasizes habits and goals more than demographic labels.
risk_notes: Casting alone is weaker evidence than repeated motivation and context cues.
